lessons.sub: Why security people use Python, and how to store a value.
learn: Key terms

Script: a short program saved in a file that automates a task.
Interpreter: the program that reads your Python code and runs it.
Variable: a name that stores a value so you can use it later.
Comment: a note in your code that Python ignores.
Why Python

Python is one of the most popular scripting languages in security. Analysts use it to read logs, automate checks and connect tools. They also call application programming interfaces (APIs), which let programs ask other systems for data. Kali already has Python 3 installed.
Two ways to run it

You can run Python in two ways. Type `python3` to open the interactive prompt, where you try one line at a time. Leave it with `exit()`. Or save your code in a file ending in .py, then run `python3 hello.py`.
print and comments
`print()` shows output on screen. Python ignores anything after `#`, so you can use it to write a comment. Use comments to explain why the code does something, not what it does.

# Say hello to the SOC
print("Hello, SOC")
print(2 + 3)
Variables
A variable is a name for a value. You create one with `=`, which assigns the value to the name. Choose names that say what the value is, like `target_ip`, not `x`.

target_ip = "10.10.10.20"
port = 445
print(target_ip, port)
The core types
Every value has a type, which is the kind of value it is. `str` is text, `int` is a whole number, `float` has a decimal point and `bool` is True or False. `type()` tells you which one you have.

play.p: Change the message and the port, then tap Run.
play.code:
host = "10.10.10.20"
port = 445
print("Checking", host, "on port", port)

real: On the job

A security operations centre (SOC) analyst gets 2,000 alerts exported to a file. Reading them by hand takes a day. A 15-line script sorts and counts them in a second. That's why so many security job ads mention Python.
myth: You have to be a programmer to use Python in security.
Most security scripts are short. They read something, filter it, count it and print it. You'll write useful ones by the end of this track.

tryit.p: Create a file, run it, then change the message and run it again.
tryit.code:
echo 'print("Hello from Kali")' > hello.py
python3 hello.py

quiz.w: 5. The second line is a comment, so only `print(2 + 3)` runs. Not 2 + 3: print shows the result, not the sum as written. Not 10: Python ignores the commented line.
<class 'float'>. The decimal point makes it a float, even though the value is a whole number. Not int: 3.0 has a decimal point. Not 3: `type()` gives the type, not the value.

quiz.q: How do you run a script saved as scan.py?
quiz.w: python3 scan.py. Give the file to the python3 interpreter, which runs it. Not run or print: neither of these starts the Python interpreter.

challenge.p: Set `target` to `"win10"`, then print `Target: win10`.
challenge.hint: Put the text between the quotes on the first line.
challenge.solution:
target = "win10"
print("Target:", target)

recap: Python is one of the most popular scripting languages in security.
Run it with `python3` or `python3 file.py`.
`print()` shows output; `#` starts a comment.
Assign with `=` and use descriptive names.
`type()` shows whether a value is str, int, float or bool.

lessons.sub: Text, numbers, and building readable output.
learn: Key terms

String: a piece of text, such as a username or a log line.
Integer: a whole number, such as a port number.
f-string: a string with an f before the quotes, which fills in values from braces.
Text isn't a number
Anything you read from a file, a log or user input arrives as text. Adding text joins it, so "22" + "1" gives "221". Convert with `int()` before doing maths.
Converting
`int("22")` turns text into a number, and `str(22)` turns a number into text. Converting text that isn't a number, like `int("ssh")`, raises a ValueError.
f-strings
Put an f before the opening quote. Python then replaces any variable inside braces with its value. f-strings are the clearest way to build output and messages.

ip = "10.10.10.20"
open_ports = 3
print(f"{ip} has {open_ports} open ports")

play.p: Edit the values and run it again. Then try a calculation inside the braces.
play.code:
ip = "10.10.10.20"
open_ports = 3
print(f"{ip} has {open_ports} open ports")
print(f"Next port: {22 + 1}")

real: On the job

A firewall export lists ports as text. A script that checks `"80" > "443"` says True. Text compares one character at a time, and 8 comes after 4. As numbers, 80 > 443 is False, so converting to int first fixes it.
myth: Python works out what you meant, so types don't matter.
Python won't guess. Mixing text and numbers either raises an error or quietly gives the wrong result.

tryit.p: Type each line into the Python prompt and predict the result before you press Enter.

quiz.w: 221. Both values are text, so `+` joins them. Not 23: that needs `int()` to turn the text into a number first. Not an error: joining two strings is allowed.
23. `int()` converts the text to a number first, so this is real addition. Not 221: that's what joining two strings gives. Not an error: "22" is valid number text, so the conversion works.

Scanning 10.10.10.20. The f prefix fills in the braces with the variable's value. Not Scanning {ip}: you'd only see the braces without the f. Not the version with the f and quotes: print shows the text, not the code.

challenge.p: The log gives the port as text. Add 1 to it as a number, then use an f-string to print `next port: 23`.
challenge.hint: Convert with `int(port)` inside the braces.
challenge.solution:
port = "22"
print(f"next port: {int(port) + 1}")

recap: Input from files, logs and users arrives as text.
Convert with `int()` and `str()` before mixing.
f-strings put values inside `{}`.
You can do maths inside the braces.

lessons.sub: Make decisions in code.
learn: Key terms

Condition: a check that is either True or False.
Block: the indented lines that belong to an if, a loop or a function.
Branch: one of the paths code can take, such as the if or the else.
Indentation: spaces at the start of a line that show which block it belongs to.
if, elif, else
An if runs its block only when its condition is true. elif checks the next condition, and else catches everything left. Only the first matching branch runs.
Comparisons
`==` means equal and `!=` means not equal. `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=` compare numbers. Combine conditions with `and`, `or` and `not`.
Indentation is syntax

Python groups code by indentation, not braces. Lines inside an if or a loop are indented, usually by four spaces. Python needs the indentation to be consistent. Getting it wrong is an error, not a style issue.

play.p: Change `fails` to 2, 6 and 12 and see which branch runs.

real: On the job

Every alert rule is an if statement underneath. For example, if failed logins from one IP go over a threshold in five minutes, raise an alert. Tuning that threshold is a daily job in a security operations centre (SOC).
myth: `=` and `==` mean the same thing.
`=` stores a value; `==` compares two values. Writing `if fails = 5:` is a syntax error in Python.

quiz.w: ok. 3 isn't over 5 or 10, so the else branch runs. Not warn or block: those need more than 5 or 10.

quiz.q: What happens when you run this?
quiz.w: An IndentationError. The body of an if must be indented, so Python refuses to run the file. Not hi or nothing: Python stops before it runs any line.
admin. `role` equals "admin", so the `==` check is True and the first branch runs. Not user: else only runs when the check is False. Not nothing: with an else, one branch runs.

challenge.p: `cvss` holds a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) score from 0 to 10. Print `high` if it's 7.0 or more, otherwise print `low`.
challenge.hint: Use `if cvss >= 7.0:` with an `else:`. Indent each print by four spaces.

recap: if, elif and else choose one branch.
`==` compares; `=` assigns.
Combine conditions with and, or and not.
Indentation decides what's inside the if.
Rules and alerts are conditions underneath.

lessons.sub: Keep many values in order.
learn: Key terms

List: an ordered collection of items inside square brackets.
Index: an item's position in a list, counting from 0.
Slice: a part of a list, picked out by a start and an end position.
Lists
A list holds items in order, inside square brackets. You get an item by its index, which starts at 0.

ports = [22, 80, 443]
print(ports[0], ports[2])
Changing a list
`.append(x)` adds an item to the end. `.remove(x)` takes out the first item that matches. `len(ports)` tells you how many items there are.

ports = [22, 80]
ports.append(443)
ports.remove(80)
print(ports, len(ports))
Slicing
`ports[0:2]` gives the first two items. The start is included and the end isn't. You'll see the same rule with `range` in the next lesson.

ports = [21, 22, 80, 443]
print(ports[0:2], ports[-1])
Counting from the end
A negative index counts back from the end of the list. `ports[-1]` is the last item.

play.p: Add another port to the list, then print the last one.
play.code:
ports = [22, 80, 443]
ports.append(3389)
print(ports)
print("last:", ports[-1])

real: On the job

A scanner reports the open ports on each host as a list. You compare that list with the ports you expect. Then you append anything unexpected to a findings list. This is a daily vulnerability management job.
myth: The first item in a list is item 1.
Python counts from 0, so `ports[0]` is the first item and `ports[1]` is the second.

quiz.w: 80. Index 1 is the second item, because counting starts at 0. Not 22: that's index 0. Not 443: that's index 2.
[22, 443]. `.remove(80)` takes 80 out, leaving 22 and 443. Not [80, 443]: remove takes out the value you give it, not the first item. Not [22, 80, 443]: the list does change.
[21, 22]. The slice starts at index 0 and stops before index 2. Not [22, 80]: the start index is included, and index 0 is 21. Not [21, 22, 80]: the end index isn't included.

challenge.p: Add 3389 to the list, then print how many ports there are.
challenge.hint: Use `.append(3389)` then `print(len(ports))`.
challenge.solution:
ports = [22, 80, 443]
ports.append(3389)
print(len(ports))

recap: Lists hold ordered items.
Indexes start at 0.
`.append()` adds; `.remove()` takes out.
Slices include the start, not the end.
Index -1 is the last item.

lessons.sub: Do the same thing to every item.
learn: Key terms

Loop: code that repeats a block, such as once for each host or log line.
range: a built-in that produces a run of whole numbers.
Filtering: keeping only the items that match a condition.
for loops
A for loop runs its indented block once for each item. This is how you check every host, every port or every log line.

for port in [22, 80, 443]:
    print("checking", port)
Keeping a count
To keep a running count, write `count += 1` inside the loop. It's short for `count = count + 1`.
range
`range(1, 5)` produces 1, 2, 3 and 4. It's handy for port ranges and counting.
Filtering as you go
Combine a loop and an if to keep only what matters. Build a new list of the matches, then work with that list.

play.p: Change the list and the condition, then run it.

real: On the job
A vulnerability scanner returns 500 findings. A loop keeps only the critical ones on internet-facing hosts. That gives you a short list to fix first.
myth: `range(1, 5)` includes 5.
The stop value is excluded, so `range(1, 5)` gives 1 to 4. For ports 1 to 1024, write `range(1, 1025)`.

tryit.p: Loop over your lab addresses and print a line for each. Then change it to skip the Kali address (10.10.10.10).

quiz.w: [1, 2, 3]. The start is included and the stop is not. Not [0, 1, 2, 3]: this range starts at 1, not 0. Not [1, 2, 3, 4]: 4 is the stop value, so it's left out.

quiz.code:
total = 0
for n in [3, 4, 5]:
    total = total + n
print(total)
quiz.w: 12. The loop adds each number to the running total: 3, then 7, then 12. Not 5: that's only the last number. Not 345: these are numbers, so they're added, not joined like text.

quiz.code:
count = 0
for n in range(1, 4):
    count += 1
print(count)
quiz.w: 3. The loop runs for 1, 2 and 3, adding 1 to `count` each time. Not 1 or 2: the range gives three numbers, so the loop runs three times.

challenge.p: Loop over the list and print only the ports below 1024, one per line.
challenge.hint: Use `for p in ports:` and inside it `if p < 1024:`.

recap: for loops run once per item.
`count += 1` adds one each time round.
`range(a, b)` stops before b.
A loop plus an if filters a list.

lessons.sub: Look things up by name.
learn: Key terms

Dictionary: a collection that maps keys to values, inside curly braces.
Key: the name you use to look up a value in a dictionary.
KeyError: the error Python raises when you look up a key that isn't there.
JavaScript Object Notation (JSON): a text format for structured, nested data.
Dictionaries
A dictionary maps keys to values, inside curly braces. You look up a value by its key. It works like the Domain Name System (DNS), which looks up an address by name.

services = {22: "ssh", 80: "http", 443: "https"}
print(services[443])
Safe lookups
Looking up a missing key with square brackets raises a KeyError. `.get(key, default)` returns the default instead. That's safer with messy data.
Counting by hand
To count things, add 1 to a key's value each time you see that key. Use `.get()` to start missing keys at 0.

play.p: Add another service, then look up one that isn't there.

real: On the job

Once parsed, JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) data from a security application programming interface (API) becomes Python dictionaries. Knowing how to reach `alert["src"]["ip"]` reliably is a core skill in automation scripts.
myth: Dictionaries are only for advanced code.
They're one of the most useful beginner tools. Look-up tables, counts and JSON data read into Python are all dictionaries.

quiz.w: unknown. 443 isn't a key, so `.get()` returns the default you gave it. Not None: that's only returned when you give no default. Not a KeyError: only square brackets raise that.

o: A new IP isn't a key yet
quiz.w: A new IP isn't a key yet. Square brackets on a missing key raise a KeyError. `.get` starts new keys at 0. Not speed or sorting: `.get` does neither.
KeyError. Square brackets raise KeyError for a missing key, and the except block prints that text. Not None or unknown: only `.get()` returns a default.

challenge.p: Count how many times each user appears and print the dictionary.
challenge.hint: Loop over `users` and use `counts[u] = counts.get(u, 0) + 1`.

recap: A dictionary maps keys to values.
`.get(key, default)` avoids KeyErrors.
Count with `.get(k, 0) + 1`.
API data usually arrives as dictionaries.

lessons.sub: Package code you'll reuse.
learn: Key terms

Function: a named block of code that you can run again and again.
Parameter: a name in a function's brackets that receives a value when the function is called.
Return value: the result a function sends back with return.
Default value: the value a parameter uses when the caller leaves it out.
Functions
`def` defines a function, which is a named block you can call again and again. Parameters go in the brackets. `return` sends a result back to the caller.
Why functions matter
Functions stop you copying code around. Fix a bug once, and every caller gets the fix. Functions also make scripts easier to test and read.
Parameters and defaults
A parameter can have a default value, as in `def check(port, timeout=1):`. Callers can leave it out, or pass their own value.

def check(port, timeout=1):
    return f"port {port}, timeout {timeout}"

print(check(22))
print(check(22, 5))

play.p: Change the threshold, or call the function with different numbers.
play.code:
def suspicious(fails, threshold=5):
    return fails > threshold

print(suspicious(3))
print(suspicious(8))
print(suspicious(8, threshold=10))

real: On the job

Detection rules work like functions. Given an event, they return True if it's suspicious. Small functions like `is_off_hours(timestamp)` are exactly how logic is built in security information and event management (SIEM) tools. The same goes for security orchestration, automation and response (SOAR) tools.
myth: A function that prints a result returns it too.
Printing shows a value on screen. Returning hands it back to the caller. A function without return gives back None.

tryit.p: Write a function that flags a login as suspicious after more than five failures. Then test it with a few values.

quiz.w: 12. The function multiplies the two values passed in and returns 12. Not 7: that's 3 plus 4, but the code multiplies. Not 34: these are numbers, so they aren't joined like text.

quiz.code:
def check(port):
    print("checked", port)

result = check(22)
print(result)
quiz.w: checked 22, then None. The function prints but never returns, so `result` is None. Not 22: printing a value doesn't return it. Not None only: the print inside the function still runs first.
port 22, timeout 1. `timeout` wasn't passed, so it uses its default of 1. Not timeout 5: this call doesn't pass 5. Not an error: the default makes that parameter optional.

challenge.p: Write a function `is_admin_port(port)` that returns True for 22, 3389 and 5985. Then print `is_admin_port(3389)`.
challenge.hint: Replace `pass` with `return port in (22, 3389, 5985)`.

recap: `def` packages code; `return` hands back a result.
Fix a bug once and every caller gets the fix.
Defaults make parameters optional.
A function without return gives back None.
Small functions make detection logic readable.

lessons.sub: Clean, split and search text.
learn: Key terms

Method: a function that belongs to a value, called with a dot after the value.
Whitespace: spaces, tabs and newlines.
Case-sensitive: treating upper-case and lower-case letters as different.
String methods
Strings come with built-in methods. `.lower()` and `.upper()` change case. `.strip()` removes spaces and newlines from the ends. `.replace()` swaps one piece of text for another.

user = "  Admin \n"
print(user.strip().lower())
Split into parts
`.split()` breaks a string into a list of words. Give it a character, and it splits on that character instead. It's the quickest way to pull fields out of a log line.

line = "Failed password for root from 10.0.0.5"
parts = line.split()
print(parts[-1])
Searching
`in` checks whether text appears anywhere in a string. `.startswith()` and `.endswith()` check the start and the end. All of them are case-sensitive.

play.p: Change the log line and see what each method gives you.
play.code:
line = "  Failed password for ROOT from 10.0.0.5  "
clean = line.strip().lower()
print(clean)
print(clean.split()[-1])
print(clean.startswith("failed"))

real: On the job

Checking reported phishing emails often starts with string checks. Does the sender's domain end with your company's domain, or with a look-alike? A couple of `.endswith()` and `.lower()` calls handle that.
myth: `in` and `==` do the same thing.
`==` needs an exact match. `in` finds text anywhere, so "admin" in "sysadmin" is True. That difference causes real filtering bugs.

tryit.h: Pull fields from a log line
tryit.p: Split a realistic Secure Shell (SSH) log line, then print the user and IP address.
tryit.code:
line = "Failed password for invalid user test from 10.10.10.10 port 51234 ssh2"
parts = line.split()
print("user:", parts[5])
print("ip:", parts[7])

quiz.w: for. Counting starts at 0, so Failed is 0, password is 1 and for is 2. Not password: that's index 1. Not root: that's index 3.
True. `in` matches anywhere inside the string, which is easy to forget when filtering usernames. Not False: "sysadmin" contains "admin". Not an error: `in` works on any two strings.

True. `.endswith` checks the end of the text exactly, and this address ends with @contoso.com. Not False or an error: the match is exact and valid. The `@` matters, because without it, `evilcontoso.com` would match too.

challenge.p: Print just the username from this log line, in lower case: `root`.
challenge.hint: `.split()` gives a list of words. The username is at index 3. Then use `.lower()`.
challenge.solution:
line = "Failed password for ROOT from 10.0.0.5"
print(line.split()[3].lower())

recap: `.strip()`, `.lower()` and `.split()` do most clean-up.
Split, then pick the part you need.
`.startswith()` and `.endswith()` check the start and end.
`in` matches anywhere; `==` needs an exact match.

lessons.t: Parse a log: failed SSH logins
lessons.sub: Count failed Secure Shell (SSH) logins in a realistic log.
learn: Key terms

Parse: to pull useful fields out of text, such as a log line.
with statement: Python code that sets something up, such as an open file, and cleans it up when its block ends.
Newline: the hidden character that ends each line of text.
Open files with with
`with open(path) as f:` opens a file. It closes the file automatically when the block ends, even if an error happens. Use it every time.
Line by line
Looping over a file gives you one line at a time. Each line still ends with a newline. `.strip()` removes it before you print or compare the line.
Messy logs
Real logs contain odd characters. `open(path, errors="replace")` swaps unreadable bytes for a placeholder. That stops the script crashing halfway through.
Practise on text first
Here, a sample log is stored in a variable. `.splitlines()` turns it into lines. On Kali you'd loop over an open file instead, and the loop body stays the same.

play.p: The sample log is in `LOG`. Run it, then change what it counts, for example to `Accepted`.
play.code:
LOG = """Nov 17 09:14:01 kali sshd[812]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50122 ssh2
Nov 17 09:14:05 kali sshd[812]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50124 ssh2
Nov 17 09:15:12 kali sshd[815]: Accepted publickey for kane from 10.10.10.10 port 51000 ssh2
Nov 17 09:16:40 kali sshd[818]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 198.51.100.23 port 40001 ssh2
Nov 17 09:16:44 kali sshd[818]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50130 ssh2"""
count = 0
for line in LOG.splitlines():
    if "Failed password" in line:
        count += 1
print(count, "failed logins")

real: On the job

An incident responder receives a 2 GB web server log. Opening it in Notepad freezes the laptop. A Python loop reads it line by line and keeps only requests from the suspect IP. Then it writes them to a small file.
myth: You must load the whole file before searching it.
Looping over the file object reads one line at a time. That's faster to start, and it works on files bigger than your random access memory (RAM).

tryit.p: SSH isn't running on Kali by default. Start it, fail a login and export the log. Then count the failures with Python.
tryit.code:
sudo systemctl start ssh
ssh nobody@localhost    # type yes, a wrong password, then Ctrl+C
sudo journalctl -u ssh > ssh.log
python3 -c '
count = 0
with open("ssh.log", errors="replace") as f:
    for line in f:
        if "Failed password" in line:
            count += 1
print(count, "failed logins")
'
sudo systemctl stop ssh

quiz.q: What does `with open(...) as f:` give you that plain `open()` doesn't?
o: It opens the file more quickly
quiz.w: It closes the file automatically. The with block guarantees the file is closed when the block ends, even if an error interrupts it. Not speed: with doesn't change how fast a file opens. Not encryption: with doesn't change the contents.

quiz.q: Why loop over a log file line by line instead of reading it all at once?
o: It sorts the lines by time
quiz.w: It works on huge files, even ones bigger than memory. Only one line is held at a time, so file size stops mattering. Not sorting or removing duplicates: the loop reads every line in its original order.
2. Two lines contain "Failed", so the count goes up twice. Not 3: the Accepted line doesn't match. Not 1: the loop checks every line.

challenge.p: Print the source IP of every failed login, one per line, repeats included. The IP is the word after `from`.
challenge.start:
LOG = """Nov 17 09:14:01 kali sshd[812]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50122 ssh2
Nov 17 09:14:05 kali sshd[812]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50124 ssh2
Nov 17 09:15:12 kali sshd[815]: Accepted publickey for kane from 10.10.10.10 port 51000 ssh2
Nov 17 09:16:40 kali sshd[818]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 198.51.100.23 port 40001 ssh2
Nov 17 09:16:44 kali sshd[818]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50130 ssh2"""
for line in LOG.splitlines():
    if "Failed password" in line:
        parts = line.split()
challenge.hint: `parts.index("from")` gives the position of `from`, so the IP is at that position plus 1.
challenge.solution:
LOG = """Nov 17 09:14:01 kali sshd[812]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50122 ssh2
Nov 17 09:14:05 kali sshd[812]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50124 ssh2
Nov 17 09:15:12 kali sshd[815]: Accepted publickey for kane from 10.10.10.10 port 51000 ssh2
Nov 17 09:16:40 kali sshd[818]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 198.51.100.23 port 40001 ssh2
Nov 17 09:16:44 kali sshd[818]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50130 ssh2"""
for line in LOG.splitlines():

recap: Always open files with `with`.
Loop line by line; never load a huge log at once.
`.strip()` removes the newline at the end of each line.
Find the field by a nearby word, not a fixed position.
`errors="replace"` survives messy logs.

lessons.sub: Remove duplicates and compare groups.
learn: Key terms

Set: a collection of unique values with no fixed order.
Asset inventory: a list of every system and device an organisation owns.
Shadow IT: devices or software that people use without the organisation's approval.
What a set is
A set holds unique values with no fixed order. `set(ips)` throws away duplicates, so `len(set(ips))` counts the distinct IPs.
Comparing sets
`a - b` is what's in a but not b. `a & b` is what's in both. That's how you compare what a scanner found with your asset inventory.
Sorting for output
A set's printed order can change from run to run. Use `sorted(myset)` when you want stable, readable output.

play.p: Change the lists and see which hosts are unknown.

real: On the job

Comparing the hosts on the network with the hosts in the asset inventory is how shadow IT is found. Shadow IT means devices or software used without approval. With sets, it's one line: `seen - assets`.
myth: A set keeps items in the order you added them.
A set doesn't promise any order. If the order you added items matters, use a list instead.

quiz.w: 2. The set keeps one copy of each address, so there are two. Not 3: that counts the duplicate as well. Not 1: 1.1.1.1 and 2.2.2.2 are different addresses.
{3}. `a - b` keeps what's only in a, and 3 is the only value b doesn't have. Not {1, 2}: that's the overlap, which & gives. Not {1, 2, 3, 4}: that's everything in either set.

quiz.q: Why print `sorted(myset)` instead of the set itself?
quiz.w: Sets have no fixed order. Sorting gives stable, readable output each time. Not that sets can't be printed: they can, in any order. Not duplicates: the set has already removed them.

challenge.p: Print the unique failed-login IPs, sorted, as a list.
challenge.hint: `sorted(set(fails))` removes duplicates and sorts in one go.

recap: Sets keep one copy of each value.
`a - b` finds what's missing; `a & b` finds the overlap.
Sets have no order, so sort before printing.
Sets are great for comparing asset lists.

lessons.sub: Count things in one line.
learn: Key terms

Module: a file of ready-made Python code that you load with import.
Counter: a tool in the collections module that counts how often each item appears.
Top talkers: the hosts that send or receive the most traffic.
Counter does it for you
`collections.Counter` counts every item in a list in one line. It's perfect for top talkers and top failed-login sources.

from collections import Counter
fails = ["1.1.1.1", "2.2.2.2", "1.1.1.1"]
print(Counter(fails).most_common(1))
most_common
`.most_common(n)` gives the top n. For example, `Counter(ips).most_common(3)` gives the top three as (value, count) pairs, already sorted. Use it for a "top attackers" report.
Counters add up
You can update a Counter as you go with `c[ip] += 1`. A missing key starts at 0, so there's no KeyError.

play.p: Change the list and the number passed to `most_common`.
play.code:
from collections import Counter
ips = ["203.0.113.7", "198.51.100.23", "203.0.113.7", "203.0.113.7", "192.0.2.4"]
for ip, n in Counter(ips).most_common(2):
    print(ip, n)

real: On the job
"Which IPs failed to log in the most last night?" is a daily question in a security operations centre (SOC). Read the log, pull out the IPs and put them in a Counter. Then print `most_common(10)`.

tryit.p: Count how often each IP appears and print the top two.
tryit.code:
from collections import Counter
ips = ["10.10.10.20", "10.10.10.30", "10.10.10.20", "8.8.8.8", "10.10.10.20"]
for ip, n in Counter(ips).most_common(2):
    print(ip, n)

myth: You need a database to count events.
For millions of lines, maybe. For a day's authentication log, a Counter in memory is instant.

quiz.w: [('a', 2)]. `most_common` returns a list of (item, count) pairs, highest first. Not {'a': 2}: that's a dictionary, not a list. Not just a: the result includes the count as well as the item.

quiz.code:
from collections import Counter
c = Counter()
c["root"] += 1
print(c["root"])
quiz.w: 1. Missing keys start at 0 in a Counter, so adding 1 gives 1. Not 0: the line that adds 1 did run. Not a KeyError: a Counter treats a missing key as 0.
('a', 3). `most_common(1)` returns a list holding the top pair; `[0]` takes that pair out. Not ('b', 2): b appears less often than a. Not 3: you get the whole pair, not just the count.

challenge.p: Print the single most-targeted username and its count, like `root 3`.
challenge.hint: `Counter(users).most_common(1)[0]` gives a (name, count) pair.
challenge.solution:
from collections import Counter
users = ["root", "admin", "root", "test", "root", "admin"]
name, n = Counter(users).most_common(1)[0]
print(name, n)

recap: Counter counts a list in one line.
`most_common(n)` gives the top n.
Missing keys start at 0.
Use it for top-attacker reports.

lessons.sub: Find patterns, not just fixed text.
learn: Key terms

Regular expression (regex): a pattern that matches text.
Raw string: a string with r before the quotes, which keeps backslashes exactly as typed.
Capture group: brackets in a pattern that save part of the match.
Escape: putting a backslash before a character so it's matched literally.
What regex is
A regular expression (regex) is a pattern that matches text. Python's `re` module uses it to find IP addresses, usernames or error codes inside messy lines.
Raw strings
Write patterns as raw strings, like `r"..."`. The r stops Python treating backslashes as its own escapes.
Building blocks
`\d` matches a digit, and `\S` matches any non-whitespace character. `+` means one or more. `.` matches any character except a newline, so escape it as `\.` when you mean a real dot.
Capture groups
Brackets in a pattern capture part of the match. `re.search` returns a match object, which holds the result. `.group(1)` gives you what the first brackets captured.

import re
line = "Failed password for root from 10.0.0.5 port 22"
m = re.search(r"from (\S+)", line)
if m:
    print(m.group(1))
findall
`re.findall` returns every match in the text as a list. It's the quickest way to pull all the IP addresses or numbers out of a line.
Check what you match
A simple IP pattern also matches impossible values like 999.999.999.999. Check your results with the `ipaddress` module.

play.p: Add more addresses to the text and run it again.
play.code:
import re
text = "Blocked 10.10.10.10 and 203.0.113.7; allowed 10.10.10.20"
print(re.findall(r"\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+", text))

real: On the job

Threat intelligence reports list indicators, such as IPs and domains, inside paragraphs of text. A regex pulls them out in seconds. Then you can block them, or search for them in your security information and event management (SIEM) system.
myth: You need to memorise regex syntax.
Most people don't. Learn the few building blocks here, then test patterns on a site like regex101 or in the Python prompt.

quiz.code:
import re
m = re.search(r"from (\S+)", "Failed password for root from 10.0.0.5 port 22")
print(m.group(1))
quiz.w: 10.0.0.5. The brackets capture the non-space text right after "from ". Not root: the pattern looks after from, not before it. Not from 10.0.0.5: group 1 holds only what the brackets captured.
['22', '443']. findall returns every match as a string inside a list. Not [22, 443]: regex matches are text, not numbers. Not 22443: the matches stay as separate items in the list.

quiz.q: Why write the pattern as `r"\d+"` instead of `"\d+"`?
o: It makes the pattern run faster
The r keeps backslashes exactly as typed
quiz.w: The r keeps backslashes exactly as typed. A raw string stops Python treating backslashes as its own escapes. Without it, `\b` (a regex word boundary) silently becomes a backspace character. Not case or speed: the r changes neither.

challenge.p: Use a capture group to print the IP after `from` in this line.
challenge.start:
import re
line = "Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50122 ssh2"
challenge.hint: `re.search(r"from (\S+)", line)` then `.group(1)`.
challenge.solution:
import re
line = "Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50122 ssh2"
m = re.search(r"from (\S+)", line)
print(m.group(1))

recap: `re.search` finds the first match; `re.findall` finds them all.
Capture groups pull out just the part you need.
Use raw strings for patterns.
Escape a real dot as `\.`.
Check IP matches with the `ipaddress` module.

lessons.sub: Combine checks into one useful tool.
learn: Key terms

Passphrase: a long password made of several words.
Breached-password list: a list of passwords already exposed in data breaches.
any(): a built-in function that returns True if at least one item is True.
Length matters most
Length matters most in a password. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) covers this in SP 800-63B-4 (2025). It requires at least 15 characters when a password is the only factor.
No forced symbols or changes
NIST SP 800-63B-4 bans forced symbol rules. It also bans routine password changes.
Checks with any()
`any(c.isdigit() for c in pw)` is True if at least one character is a digit. Read it as: for each character c, is it a digit? The same pattern works with `.isupper()` and `.islower()`.
Keep it honest
A checker can only guess. A long password that's already in a breach list is still weak. That's why NIST requires checks against breached-password lists.

play.p: Try different passwords and watch the score change.
play.code:
pw = "Summer2024"
score = 0
if len(pw) >= 12: score += 1
if any(c.isdigit() for c in pw): score += 1
if any(c.isupper() for c in pw): score += 1
if pw.lower() not in ["password", "summer2024", "letmein"]: score += 1
print(pw, "scores", score, "out of 4")

real: On the job
Help desk staff often get asked "is this a good password?" Interviewers ask about it too. The key point is that length and breach checks matter more than symbols.
myth: Adding a symbol makes any password strong.
"P@ssw0rd!" has symbols and is in every breach list. Length and uniqueness matter more.

quiz.code:
pw = "hunter9"
print(any(c.isdigit() for c in pw))
quiz.w: True. "9" is a digit, so `any()` finds at least one. Not False: one digit is enough. Not 9: `any()` returns True or False, not the matching character.

o: Your old password with the year changed
quiz.w: A long, unique passphrase. Length and uniqueness beat complexity rules. Not the 8-character password: it's short, and a symbol adds little. Not the old password with a new year: attackers guess that change easily.
False. "abc" has no upper-case letters, so no character passes the check. Not True: that needs at least one upper-case letter. Not an error: `any()` works on any string.

challenge.p: Write `strong(pw)` that returns True only if the password is at least 15 characters long. That's NIST's minimum when a password is the only factor. Print `strong("correct horse battery")`.
challenge.hint: `return len(pw) >= 15`

recap: Length matters most.
NIST bans forced symbol rules and routine changes.
`any(... for c in pw)` checks for a type of character.
A checker estimates; it can't prove strength.
Check against breached-password lists.

lessons.sub: Fingerprint text and files.
learn: Key terms

Hash: a short fingerprint of data that changes if the data changes.
Bytes: raw data stored as numbers from 0 to 255.
Hex digest: a hash written as hexadecimal text, using 0 to 9 and a to f.
Salt: a random value added to each password before hashing, so identical passwords get different hashes.
hashlib

Python's `hashlib` module computes hashes such as SHA-256, a Secure Hash Algorithm (SHA) with a 256-bit result. Hash functions work on bytes, so turn text into bytes first with `.encode()`. Then `.hexdigest()` gives the familiar hex string.

import hashlib
print(hashlib.sha256("hello".encode()).hexdigest())
Hashing a file

Open the file in binary mode and feed it to the hash in chunks. Chunks stop large files filling memory. Compare the result with the publisher's hash to check integrity. A tiny change to the file gives a completely different hash.
Passwords need more
SHA-256 is too fast for storing passwords. Use a slow, salted algorithm such as Argon2 or bcrypt instead. Use Argon2 via a library like argon2-cffi, and never write your own.

play.p: Change one letter of the text and see how much the hash changes.
play.code:
import hashlib
print(hashlib.sha256("hello".encode()).hexdigest())
print(hashlib.sha256("hellp".encode()).hexdigest())

real: On the job
Malware analysts share file hashes, not files. Search for a file's SHA-256 in a threat intelligence service. In seconds, you'll see whether a suspicious attachment is already known to be malicious.

tryit.p: Hash any file, then run `sha256sum` on the same file. The two results should match exactly.
tryit.code:
import hashlib, sys
h = hashlib.sha256()
with open(sys.argv[1], "rb") as f:
    for chunk in iter(lambda: f.read(65536), b""):
        h.update(chunk)
print(h.hexdigest())
# run: python3 hashfile.py /etc/hostname
# compare: sha256sum /etc/hostname

myth: A hash can be reversed to get the original back.
A hash is one-way. Attackers "crack" hashes by guessing inputs and hashing each guess. That's why slow password hashes matter.

quiz.w: 64. SHA-256 gives 256 bits, which is 32 bytes, and each byte is 2 hex characters. Not 32: that's the length in bytes. Not 256: that's the length in bits.

quiz.q: Which should you use to store user passwords?
quiz.w: Argon2 or bcrypt. They're slow and salted, so stolen hashes are expensive to crack. Not SHA-256 on its own: it's too fast. Not Base64: it's encoding, so anyone can reverse it.
hashlib needs bytes, not text. `.encode()` turns text into bytes using UTF-8. Not encryption: anyone can turn the bytes back into text. Not shorter: a SHA-256 hash has the same length for any input.

challenge.p: Print the first 8 characters of the SHA-256 hash of `abc`.
challenge.hint: Get the hex digest, then slice it with `[:8]`.
challenge.solution:
import hashlib
print(hashlib.sha256("abc".encode()).hexdigest()[:8])

recap: Hashes work on bytes: `.encode()` text first.
A tiny change gives a completely different hash.
Hash big files in chunks, in binary mode.
Passwords need Argon2 or bcrypt.

lessons.sub: Encoding you'll see in logs and phishing, and why it isn't security.
learn: Key terms

Encoding: changing data into another format that anyone can reverse, with no key.
Base64: an encoding that turns bytes into plain text characters.
Triage: a quick first check of an alert to decide how serious it is.
Encoding isn't encryption

Base64 turns bytes into plain text that's safe to send in email or JavaScript Object Notation (JSON). Anyone can reverse it with no key. So Base64 in a script or config file means the data is obscured, not protected.
Encode and decode
`base64.b64encode()` needs bytes, so call `.encode()` on text first. `b64decode()` accepts a Base64 string or bytes. Both return bytes, so call `.decode()` on the result to get text back.

import base64
enc = base64.b64encode("whoami".encode())
print(enc)
print(base64.b64decode(enc).decode())
Where you'll see it
Attackers use Base64 to hide commands, for example with `powershell -EncodedCommand`. Decoding is often the first step in triaging a suspicious command line.
Decoding PowerShell
PowerShell turns commands into UTF-16LE bytes, a Windows text format, then Base64. So decode it with `base64.b64decode(s).decode("utf-16-le")` to see the real command.

play.p: Decode the string, then encode a message of your own.
play.code:
import base64
print(base64.b64decode("aGVsbG8=").decode())
print(base64.b64encode("lab only".encode()).decode())

real: On the job
An endpoint detection and response (EDR) alert shows `powershell -enc` followed by a long string. Decode it with `.decode("utf-16-le")` to see the real command in seconds.
myth: Base64 hides secrets.
One line of Python reverses Base64. Attackers use it to slip past simple text filters, not to protect anything.

o: An error, because you need a key
quiz.w: hi. `b64decode` reverses the encoding, and `.decode()` turns the bytes into text. Not aGk=: that's the encoded input. Not an error: Base64 needs no key, which is why it's encoding, not encryption.

quiz.q: Can Base64 protect a stored password?
quiz.w: No, anyone can decode it. Base64 is encoding, not encryption. Not encryption: nothing secret is needed to reverse it. Not with a long key: Base64 doesn't use a key at all.
aGk=. "hi" encodes to aGk= in Base64, and `.decode()` turns the result into text. Not hi: that's the input before encoding. Not b'hi': the output is encoded, and `.decode()` gives text, not bytes.

challenge.p: Decode this string and print the hidden command.
challenge.hint: `base64.b64decode(secret).decode()`
challenge.solution:
import base64
secret = "bmV0IHVzZXI="
print(base64.b64decode(secret).decode())

recap: Base64 is reversible encoding, not encryption.
It works on bytes: encode and decode around it.
Attackers use it to hide commands.
Decoding is a normal triage step.
Decode PowerShell commands as UTF-16LE.

lessons.sub: Scripts that survive bad input.
learn: Key terms

Exception: an error that Python raises while a script runs, such as ValueError.
Traceback: the error report Python prints when an exception stops a script.
Failing open: allowing access when a security check breaks.
Exceptions
When something goes wrong, Python raises an exception, such as FileNotFoundError or ValueError. If nothing handles it, the exception stops the script and prints a traceback.
try and except
Put risky code in a try block. Handle a specific exception in the except block, so the script keeps running.
Catch specific errors
Catch only the errors you expect, such as ValueError. A bare `except:` catches everything, so it hides real bugs.
Fail closed

If a security check can't finish, decide what happens. A check that returns True ("allowed") when it hits an error is failing open. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) lists this as A10:2025 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions. Default to deny.

play.p: Change the list so every value is a number, then add more bad values.

real: On the job
A scheduled script crashes at 3am on one malformed log line. Nobody notices for a week. Handle the expected error, log it and carry on, so monitoring keeps running.
myth: Catching every exception with a bare except is the safe choice.
A bare except can even catch Ctrl+C, so you might not be able to stop a stuck script. Let real problems surface where you can see them.

quiz.w: port 8080. "8080" is all digits, so `int()` works and the except block is skipped. Not bad input: that only prints after a ValueError. Not a traceback: no exception is raised.

quiz.q: An access check hits a database error and returns True. What's wrong?
quiz.w: It fails open: an error grants access, so an outage becomes a breach. When a check can't finish, deny by default. Not speed or logging: the problem is what the check returns on error.
14. "7" converts cleanly, so no exception happens and the except block is skipped. Not 77: `int()` made it a number, so `*` multiplies. Not bad: that only prints after a ValueError.

challenge.p: Add up only the valid port numbers and print the total. Skip anything that isn't a number.
challenge.hint: Loop over values, and wrap `total += int(v)` in try/except ValueError.

recap: Exceptions stop scripts unless handled.
Catch specific errors, not everything.
A bare `except:` hides real bugs.
Security checks should fail closed: deny on error.
Skip bad lines and keep going.

lessons.t: JSON: spot "*" in an IAM policy
lessons.sub: Read security data the way APIs send it.
learn: Key terms

JavaScript Object Notation (JSON): a text format for structured, nested data.
Identity and Access Management (IAM) policy: a JSON document that says what an identity may do on which resources.
Wildcard: the * symbol, which matches everything.
JSON

Most security application programming interfaces (APIs) and cloud logs use JavaScript Object Notation (JSON). So do most security information and event management (SIEM) exports. `json.loads()` turns JSON text into Python dictionaries and lists. `json.dumps()` turns them back into text.
Reading nested data
Parsed JSON is dictionaries and lists inside each other. Reach into it one step at a time, with keys and indexes.

import json
alert = json.loads('{"rule": "brute force", "src": {"ip": "203.0.113.7"}, "count": 42}')
print(alert["src"]["ip"], alert["count"])
IAM policies are JSON
An Amazon Web Services (AWS) Identity and Access Management (IAM) policy is JSON. It holds a list of `Statement` entries.
Allowing * on *

`"Effect": "Allow"` with `"Action": "*"` on `"Resource": "*"` allows everything on everything. That breaks least privilege: giving each person and process only the access their job needs. With `"Deny"`, the same statement would block everything instead.
Pretty printing
`json.dumps(data, indent=2)` formats JSON with line breaks and indents. That makes a messy API response readable in seconds.

play.p: The policy is a JSON string. Run it, then change the second statement's Action to `s3:ListBucket`.
play.code:
import json
policy = '{"Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{"Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::reports/*"}, {"Effect": "Allow", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*"}]}'
doc = json.loads(policy)
for st in doc["Statement"]:
    print(st["Effect"], st["Action"], st["Resource"])

real: On the job
Cloud security reviews often start with "find every policy that allows `*`". A short script can check the exported IAM policies for hundreds of roles at once.
myth: JSON is a Python thing.
JSON works with almost every language, and it's used everywhere on the web. Python just maps it neatly onto dictionaries and lists.

quiz.w: 3. JSON whole numbers become Python integers, so you get the number 3. Not "3": print doesn't show quotes around text anyway. Not fails: that's the key, and indexing gives its value.
2. The Statement list holds two entries, so `len()` returns 2. Not 1: the wildcard entry is only one of the two. Not 0: the list isn't empty.

quiz.q: Why is `"Effect": "Allow"` with `"Action": "*"` on `"Resource": "*"` a problem?
quiz.w: It allows everything: admin-level rights, the opposite of least privilege. An explicit Deny, permissions boundary or service control policy (SCP) can still limit it. Not denies: the Effect is Allow. Not invalid: the JSON parses fine.

challenge.p: Print `WARNING: wildcard action` for every statement whose Action is `"*"`.
challenge.hint: Loop over `doc["Statement"]` and check `st["Action"] == "*"`. A real checker would also catch `["*"]` and `"s3:*"`.

recap: `json.loads` turns JSON text into Python data.
Reach into nested data one key at a time.
IAM policies are JSON statements.
`"Action": "*"` breaks least privilege.
`json.dumps(data, indent=2)` makes JSON readable.

lessons.sub: Subnets and private ranges without mistakes.
learn: Key terms

Subnet: a smaller network carved out of a bigger one.
Private address: an IP address reserved for use inside private networks.
Documentation range: an IP range reserved for examples, such as 203.0.113.0/24.
Global address: an IP address that's reachable on the public internet.
The ipaddress module
The `ipaddress` module understands IPv4 and IPv6. It tells you whether an address is private, and whether it sits inside a network. You don't have to split addresses on the dots by hand.

import ipaddress
ip = ipaddress.ip_address("10.10.10.20")
print(ip.is_private, ip in ipaddress.ip_network("10.10.10.0/24"))
Networks
`ipaddress.ip_network("10.10.10.0/24")` is a subnet. `ip in net` checks whether an address is inside it. `net.num_addresses` tells you its size.

import ipaddress
net = ipaddress.ip_network("10.10.10.0/24")
print(net.num_addresses, ipaddress.ip_address("10.10.10.20") in net)
Private means more than RFC 1918
`is_private` covers more than the private ranges in Request for Comments (RFC) 1918. It also covers documentation ranges like 203.0.113.0/24. This track uses that range for sample attackers.
Use is_global for the internet
To ask "is this on the internet?", use `is_global`. It's the stricter test, and documentation addresses fail it too.

play.p: Try different addresses and networks.
play.code:
import ipaddress
net = ipaddress.ip_network("192.168.1.0/28")
for ip in ["192.168.1.5", "192.168.1.20", "8.8.8.8"]:
    a = ipaddress.ip_address(ip)
    print(ip, a in net, a.is_private)

real: On the job

A security information and event management (SIEM) system exports 300 alerts as JavaScript Object Notation (JSON). A script loads them and keeps the ones whose source IP isn't private. It prints a short list of external addresses to check against threat intelligence.

tryit.p: Load a small list of alerts. Print only the ones from internet addresses, using `is_global`.

myth: Working out subnets by hand is safer.
Working them out by hand is where mistakes happen. The ipaddress module gets /27s and /29s right every time.

quiz.w: False. 8.8.8.8 is a public internet address, so it isn't private. Not True: it isn't in any private or reserved range. Not an error: `is_private` works on any valid address.

quiz.code:
import ipaddress
net = ipaddress.ip_network("192.168.1.0/26")
print(ipaddress.ip_address("192.168.1.70") in net)
quiz.w: False. A /26 starting at .0 covers .0 to .63, so .70 is outside it. Not True: .70 falls in the next /26. Not an error: checking an address against a network is valid.
16. A /28 leaves 4 host bits, and 2 to the power of 4 is 16. Not 14: that's the usable host count, but `num_addresses` counts every address. Not 32: that's the size of a /27.

challenge.p: Print only the addresses that are inside `10.10.10.0/24`, one per line.
challenge.hint: Loop, convert each with `ipaddress.ip_address(ip)`, and test `in net`.

recap: `ip_address` and `ip_network` do the maths for you.
`ip in net` checks membership.
`num_addresses` gives a subnet's size.
`is_private` includes documentation ranges.
`is_global` is stricter than `not is_private`.

lessons.sub: Filter and transform a list in one line.
learn: Key terms

List comprehension: a one-line way to build a new list from another list.
Transform: to change each item, such as making it upper case.
Nested loop: a loop inside another loop.
The pattern
A list comprehension, `[x for x in items if condition]`, builds a new list. It's the loop and if from Lesson 5, written in one line.

ports = [21, 22, 80, 443]
print([p for p in ports if p < 100])
Transforming
The first part can transform each item. For example, `[ip.strip() for ip in lines]` cleans every line at once.
Keep them readable
If a comprehension needs two conditions and a nested loop, a normal for loop is clearer. Readable beats clever.

play.p: Change the condition, or transform each item, for example `p + 1`.
play.code:
ports = [21, 22, 23, 80, 443, 3389]
print([p for p in ports if p in (21, 23)])
print([f"port-{p}" for p in ports[:2]])

real: On the job
You can often turn 300 extracted IPs into a clean list of internet IPs with one comprehension: `[ip for ip in ips if ipaddress.ip_address(ip).is_global]`.

quiz.code: print([n for n in [1, 2, 3, 4] if n % 2 == 0])
quiz.w: [2, 4]. Only even numbers pass the `n % 2 == 0` condition. Not [1, 3]: those are the odd numbers, which fail it. Not [1, 2, 3, 4]: the if filters the list, so some items are dropped.
['A', 'B']. The first part calls `.upper()` on each item, and the result is a list. Not ['a', 'b']: each item was changed. Not AB: a comprehension builds a list, not one joined string.

quiz.q: When is a normal for loop better than a comprehension?
o: When the list is very long
quiz.w: When the logic is complex. Comprehensions suit simple filters and changes, and complex logic reads better as a loop. Not list length: comprehensions work for short and long lists alike.

challenge.p: Use a comprehension to keep only the usernames that start with `adm`, then print the list.
challenge.hint: `[u for u in users if u.startswith("adm")]`
challenge.solution:
users = ["admin", "kane", "adm-backup", "guest"]
print([u for u in users if u.startswith("adm")])

recap: `[x for x in items if test]` filters.
The first part can transform each item.
Use comprehensions for simple jobs; readable beats clever.

lessons.sub: A classic cipher, and why it's easy to break.
learn: Key terms

Cipher: a method for encrypting and decrypting text.
Key space: all the possible keys a cipher can use.
Modulo: the % operator, which gives the remainder after division, such as 27 % 26 = 1.
Shifting letters
A Caesar cipher shifts each letter a fixed number of places. With a shift of 3, A becomes D. It's a teaching cipher, not real security.
Letters as numbers
`ord("a")` is 97, and `chr(97)` is "a". So you can turn a letter into a number, do maths on it and turn it back.
print(ord("a"), chr(100))
The shift formula
Shift a letter with `(ord(c) - 97 + k) % 26 + 97`, where k is the key. The `% 26` wraps z back round to a.
Why it's weak
There are only 25 possible shifts, so a loop can try them all in moments. Trying every key like this is a brute-force attack on the key space.

play.p: Change the message or the shift. A shift of -3 decrypts.

real: On the job

Nobody uses Caesar ciphers for real security. But capture the flag (CTF) challenges and malware analysis often involve simple shifts and exclusive OR (XOR) used to hide strings. Spotting and reversing them is a useful skill.
myth: A secret algorithm keeps data safe.
Security should rest on the key, not on hiding the method. This is Kerckhoffs's principle. Caesar's method being public isn't the problem. Its key space is tiny, so the key can't protect anything.

quiz.w: d. a is position 0, and a shift of 3 lands on position 3, which is d. Not c: that's a shift of 2. Not a: that would be no shift at all.
b. `% 26` wraps past z back to the start, so z shifted by 2 is b. Not |: without `% 26` you'd run past z into symbols. Not z: a shift of 2 does change the letter.

quiz.q: How many useful keys does a Caesar cipher on a to z have?
quiz.w: 25. A shift of 26 gets you back where you started, so only 25 shifts change anything. Not 26: one of those shifts changes nothing. Not 256: that's the number of values in one byte.

challenge.p: Brute-force it. Print the key (the shift) that turned `hello` into `khoor`.
challenge.hint: Loop `for k in range(26):` and print k when `caesar(secret, -k) == "hello"`.

recap: Caesar shifts letters by a fixed key.
`ord` and `chr` turn letters into numbers and back.
`% 26` wraps around the alphabet.
A tiny key space falls to brute force.
Security rests on the key, not a secret method.

lessons.sub: Spreadsheet exports are everywhere in security.
learn: Key terms

Comma-separated values (CSV): a text format for tables, with one row per line and commas between fields.
Header row: the first row of a CSV file, which names each column.
CSV injection: a spreadsheet formula hidden in a CSV cell that can run when someone opens the file.
The csv module
Python's csv module reads comma-separated values (CSV) files. `csv.DictReader` turns each row into a dictionary, keyed by the header row. So you can write `row["user"]` instead of counting columns.
Files or text
On Kali, you'd use `open("logins.csv", newline="")`. In the app, `io.StringIO(data)` makes a string behave like a file, so you can practise here.
Why not split on commas
A field like `"Smith, Jane"` contains a comma. The csv module handles the quotes correctly, but `.split(",")` breaks the field in two.
CSV injection
A cell that starts with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` can run as a formula when someone opens the CSV in Excel. If you export log data to CSV, attackers can plant those characters in usernames or URLs.

play.p: Print a different column, or filter on `result`.
play.code:
import csv, io
data = """time,user,result,src
09:01,kane,success,10.10.10.10
09:02,root,fail,203.0.113.7
09:02,root,fail,203.0.113.7
09:03,admin,fail,198.51.100.23"""
for row in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(data)):
    print(row["user"], row["result"])

real: On the job

Many tools, including Microsoft Entra ID and Okta, can export sign-in logs as CSV. For a one-off question, a short script is often faster than a security information and event management (SIEM) query. It just counts failures per user.
myth: CSV is just text, so `.split(",")` is enough.
Quoted fields can even contain line breaks, which splitting line by line gets wrong. Use the csv module and avoid subtle bugs.

quiz.code:
import csv, io
data = "user,result\nkane,success\nroot,fail"
rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(data)))
print(rows[1]["user"])
quiz.w: root. DictReader uses the header as keys, so `rows[1]` is root. Not kane: that's index 0. Not user: the header isn't a data row.

['Smith, Jane', 'admin']. The csv module keeps the quoted name together as one field. Not the three-part list: that's what splitting on commas by hand gives. Not an error: a quoted comma is valid CSV.

quiz.q: What does `csv.DictReader` use as the keys?
quiz.w: The header row. Each row becomes a dictionary keyed by the header names. Not row numbers: DictReader names fields, not positions. Not the first column: it's data, read into each dictionary like the other columns.

challenge.p: Count the failed logins and print `3 failed`.
challenge.hint: Loop over the DictReader and add 1 when `row["result"] == "fail"`.
challenge.solution:
import csv, io
data = """time,user,result,src
09:01,kane,success,10.10.10.10
09:02,root,fail,203.0.113.7
09:02,root,fail,203.0.113.7
09:03,admin,fail,198.51.100.23"""
fails = 0
for row in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(data)):
    if row["result"] == "fail":
        fails += 1
print(fails, "failed")

recap: `csv.DictReader` gives each row as a dictionary.
Use `newline=""` when opening CSV files.
Don't split on commas by hand.
Cells starting with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` can run as formulas.
Sign-in exports are often CSV.

lessons.sub: Bundle data and the code that uses it.
learn: Key terms

Class: a blueprint that describes what its objects hold and can do.
Object: one item made from a class, with its own data.
Software development kit (SDK): ready-made code for working with a service from your own programs.
What a class is
A class is a blueprint. `class Alert:` describes what every alert has (its data) and can do (its methods). Each alert you create is an object.
__init__ and self
`__init__` runs when you create an object. It stores the object's data on `self`, so `self.ip` is this alert's IP.
Methods
A method is a function inside a class that uses `self`. Calling `a.is_high()` reads naturally. It also keeps the rule next to the data it checks.

play.p: Create another alert with a different score and check it.

real: On the job

Security tools and software development kits (SDKs) hand you objects with methods. For example, boto3 gives you client and resource objects. Writing a small class yourself makes their documentation far easier to read.

quiz.w: 8. `__init__` stored 8 as `self.score`, and `a.score` reads it back. Not Alert or score: those are names, not the stored value.
False. 3 is less than 7, so `is_high` returns False. Not True: that needs 7 or more. Not None: the method returns a value.

quiz.q: What does `self` refer to inside a method?
quiz.w: The object it's called on. `a.is_high()` passes `a` in as `self`. Not the class: each object gets its own `self`. Not the last object created: `self` is whichever object you call the method on.

challenge.p: Add a method `label()` that returns `"HIGH"` when the score is 7 or more, and `"LOW"` otherwise. Then print `Alert("1.2.3.4", 9).label()`.
challenge.hint: Inside the class, add `def label(self):` and return "HIGH" if `self.score >= 7`.

recap: A class is a blueprint; objects are made from it.
`__init__` stores data on `self`.
Methods are functions that use `self`.
SDKs like boto3 are full of objects.

lessons.sub: Some code can't run in a browser, and shouldn't.
learn: Key terms

Sandbox: a protected area where code runs without access to the rest of your computer.
Socket: one end of a network connection, identified by an IP address and port.
Timeout: how long code waits for a reply before it gives up.
boto3: the official Amazon Web Services (AWS) software development kit (SDK) for Python.
The browser sandbox
In this app, Python runs inside your browser. The browser can't open raw network connections, read your files or use your Amazon Web Services (AWS) keys. That's a safety feature.
A tiny port check
This script loops over a few ports and reports the open ones. It's a Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) connect check, so the full handshake completes.

import socket
host = "10.10.10.20"
for port in [22, 135, 445, 3389]:
    s = socket.socket()
    s.settimeout(1)
    if s.connect_ex((host, port)) == 0:
        print(port, "open")
    s.close()
Connect scans and SYN scans

Nmap's default scan depends on whether you run it as root, the admin account. As root, it does a SYN scan: it sends only the first packet (SYN) and never finishes the handshake. Without root, it does a connect scan, which completes the handshake like the port-check script.
Always set a timeout
Without a timeout, a filtered port can hang your script for a long time. `s.settimeout(1)` gives up after a second. Close each socket when you're done with it.
What boto3 is
boto3 is the official AWS software development kit (SDK) for Python. Cloud security teams use it to audit settings across many accounts and services.
Installing boto3 on Kali
On Kali, install boto3 with `sudo apt install python3-boto3`. Plain pip is blocked outside a virtual environment.
Where credentials come from

boto3 finds credentials from an Identity and Access Management (IAM) role, `aws configure sso` or environment variables. Prefer short-lived credentials over long-term access keys. Never put keys in your code.
A role for audits
For audits, use a role with the AWS-managed SecurityAudit policy. Give an audit script read-only access, so a leak can't change anything.
Files need a real machine too
The browser can't read your files either. On Kali, `open(path, "w")` replaces a file's contents. `"a"` adds to the end instead, so use `"a"` for logs you add to.
real: On the job

Misconfigured cloud storage is behind many data exposures. It's A02 in the 2025 Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) Top 10. A short boto3 script that flags buckets without a public access block is a classic cloud security interview project.
myth: Writing your own scanner makes you stealthier than Nmap.
A connect scan is noisier than a SYN scan, and the target can easily log it. Use Python for automation, not stealth.

tryit.p: Only scan your own lab virtual machines (VMs). Save the port check code as portcheck.py and run it. Then compare the result with `sudo nmap -sS -p 22,135,445,3389 10.10.10.20`.
tryit.code:
python3 portcheck.py
sudo nmap -sS -p 22,135,445,3389 10.10.10.20

quiz.q: What does `connect_ex` return when a port is open?
quiz.w: 0. `connect_ex` returns an error number, and 0 means no error: the connection worked. Not 1: a non-zero number means the connection failed. Not True: it returns a number, not True or False.

o: To hide the scan from logs
quiz.w: To stop filtered ports hanging. A firewall that silently drops packets never answers, and the timeout stops your script waiting. Not encryption or hiding: a timeout only limits how long the script waits.

quiz.q: Where should a boto3 script get its AWS credentials?
o: From a comment in the script
From an IAM role or environment
Hard-coded at the top of the script
quiz.w: From an IAM role or the environment, which keeps keys out of the code. `aws configure` works too. Not hard-coded or in a comment: keys in code leak through repos and screenshots.

quiz.q: Why give an audit script a read-only role?
quiz.w: A leak can't change anything. Least privilege limits the damage if the script or its credentials are compromised. Not speed: permissions don't change how fast calls run. Not an AWS rule: you choose a role's permissions.

quiz.q: You open report.txt with mode "w". What happens to what was already in it?
o: New text is added to the end
quiz.w: It's replaced. "w" empties the file before writing. Not added to the end: that's what "a" does. Not refused: Python opens an existing file in "w" mode without complaint.

challenge.p: Don't run anything. What should a boto3 audit script use for credentials? Which permissions should its role have?
challenge.hint: Think about where secrets should never live, and about least privilege.
challenge.solution: Credentials from an IAM role or `aws configure` (never hard-coded in the script), and a read-only role with only the permissions the audit needs.

recap: Browsers can't open sockets or read your AWS keys.
A connect check completes the TCP handshake. Always set a timeout.
boto3 gets credentials from the environment or a role.
Audit with read-only roles, in accounts you own.
Mode "w" replaces a file; "a" adds to it.

lessons.sub: Put the whole track together in one tool.
learn: Key terms

Command-line argument: a value you type after the script name, such as ssh.log.
argparse: a Python module that turns command-line arguments into named values.
Threshold: the count at which a tool raises an alert.
README: a text file that explains what a project does and how to use it.
The goal
Your tool reads a Secure Shell (SSH) log and finds failed logins. It counts them per source IP and prints the IPs at or over a threshold. It uses files, regex, Counter, error handling and argparse.
The plan
Break the job into steps before writing code. Get the arguments, open the file safely, match each line, count, then report. Each step is a few lines you already know.
Command-line arguments
`argparse` turns `python3 tool.py ssh.log --threshold 5` into named values. You get help text for free. You can then reuse the script without editing the code.

import argparse
p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Count failed logins")
p.add_argument("logfile")
p.add_argument("--threshold", type=int, default=5)
args = p.parse_args()
print(args.logfile, args.threshold)
Practise here, then use Kali
Write the core here against the sample log. Then add argparse and file reading on Kali, as in the Try it card.

play.p: This is the core of the detector. Change the threshold and run it.
play.code:
import re
from collections import Counter
LOG = """Nov 17 09:14:01 kali sshd[812]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50122 ssh2
Nov 17 09:14:05 kali sshd[812]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50124 ssh2
Nov 17 09:15:12 kali sshd[815]: Accepted publickey for kane from 10.10.10.10 port 51000 ssh2
Nov 17 09:16:40 kali sshd[818]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 198.51.100.23 port 40001 ssh2
Nov 17 09:16:44 kali sshd[818]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50130 ssh2"""
pattern = re.compile(r"Failed password .* from (\S+)")
counts = Counter()
for line in LOG.splitlines():
    m = pattern.search(line)
    if m:
        counts[m.group(1)] += 1
for ip, n in counts.most_common():
    if n >= 2:
        print(f"{ip} {n} failures")

real: On the job
Interviewers love a small, working tool you can explain line by line. "I wrote a script that finds brute-force sources in SSH logs" shows Python, log analysis and security thinking at once.
myth: Portfolio projects have to be big to count.
A small tool with a clear README, sample output and an honest list of limitations beats an unfinished large one.

tryit.p: Start SSH and fail a few logins with `ssh nobody@localhost`. Then run `sudo journalctl -u ssh > ssh.log` and `python3 bruteforce.py ssh.log --threshold 2`. Stop SSH afterwards.

quiz.q: Which part of the detector pulls the source IP out of each line?
quiz.w: The capture group. `(\S+)` after "from " captures the IP, and `.group(1)` returns it. Not the Counter: it counts the IPs after they're pulled out. Not argparse: it reads command-line arguments, not the log.

quiz.q: Why compile the regex once with `re.compile` outside the loop?
o: It processes the pattern just once
quiz.w: It processes the pattern just once. Python caches patterns anyway, but compiling once is clearer and avoids repeated work on huge logs. Not case: compiling doesn't change how letters match. Not capture groups: they work without compiling.

quiz.q: Which extension would best catch a successful brute-force attack?
quiz.w: Flag a success after failures. Many failures then a success from the same source is a classic sign that a password was guessed. Not colour or sorting: they change how results look, not what you detect.

challenge.p: For each IP with 3 or more failures, print `ALERT <ip> <count>`, like `ALERT 203.0.113.7 3`. Print nothing else.
